cma:148358.texto:
East Asian paintings from China, Korea, and Japan were frequently conceived as sets of multiple images. These sets might have been composed for specific palace or temple rooms, or to portray a specific theme, such as the four seasons. Over time, the original intent of such sets is often lost through damage, changes in ownership, or a variety of other reasons. 

The identity of the artist can also be lost, but then, sometimes, retrieved. This pair of ink paintings has traditionally been labeled as Japanese and attributed to the 16th-century painter Genga. Since there are no seals or signature of the artist on the painting, this attribution was based on comparisons of brush style with paintings known to be by Genga. More recent study indicates that while the 16th century is an appropriate time frame for the pair, the precise cultural identity of the artist is not certain after all. The dark, eccentric shapes of the rocks and bamboo clusters and the dramatic tonal contrasts evident throughout the composition point to either Korean authorship or influence upon a Japanese painter of the period.
cma:148358.title: Bamboo in Rain

cma:149961.texto: This painting was part of a set of album leaves representing the Eight Views of Xiao-Xiang, a theme originating in Chinese poetry and painting that spread to both Korea and Japan. Southern China’s Xiao-Xiang area, where the mist-covered banks of the Xiang River created a complex landscape shifting like the moods and minds of people, captured the imaginations of generations of painters and calligraphers. Inscriptions on these works suggest that they were possibly ordered by newly prominent Japanese Confucian scholars.

cma:159756.texto: Muromachi period (1392–1573) artists in Japan were keenly interested in Korean and Chinese culture. Paintings from the continent were avidly collected, studied, and copied for specific techniques and effects. Most painters, however, never had the opportunity to actually travel abroad. This painting presents a typical, idealized image of a Chinese scholar's retreat in the countryside. The misty background, however, brings a decidedly Japanese element to the composition. Japanese painters had long been interested in portraying the seasons and in suggesting the special atmosphere of a place.
cma:159756.title: Thatched Hut by Water's Edge

cma:86114.texto: Hideyori is most famous as the painter of a very early pair of genre screen paintings depicting people enjoying autumn foliage at a shrine-temple complex in Mount Takao near Kyoto. In this scene, people are hard at work farming their fields and herding water buffalo in summer. Such scenes were often associated with promoting the ideal of a prosperous realm, and also with the activities of the 12 months. Historical sources are divided on the biography of painter Kano Hideyori, but many scholars now believe he was the second son of Kano Motonobu, head of the Kyoto-based Kano family atelier.
cma:86114.title: Farming and Herding Buffalo in Summer

afirmaciones.texto: Esta pintura forma parte de un conjunto que representa las Ocho Vistas de Xiao-Xiang, un tema originado en la poesía y pintura china que se difundió también en Japón y Corea.
Las inscripciones sugieren que estas obras pudieron haber sido encargadas por estudiosos confucianos japoneses, lo que indica una conexión cultural japonesa con el paisaje representado.
La obra fue propiedad de un coleccionista japonés antes de llegar al museo, lo que refuerza su vínculo con Japón.
Se observa un paisaje con elementos típicos del área de Xiao-Xiang, con bancos cubiertos de niebla y un ambiente cambiante, que es el motivo del conjunto.
Esta pareja de pinturas de tinta ha sido tradicionalmente etiquetada como japonesa y atribuida al pintor Genga del siglo XVI, aunque la identidad cultural precisa del artista no está confirmada.
El estilo de pinceladas y los contrastes tonales sugieren influencia coreana o posible autoría coreana, pero también influencia sobre un pintor japonés.
La obra proviene de una subasta en Nueva York y está en el museo de Cleveland, sin indicación directa de que represente el mismo paisaje que la imagen subida.
Se observa un paisaje con rocas y bambú, con un estilo de tinta y contrastes dramáticos, que podría relacionarse con paisajes asiáticos pero no se confirma que sea el mismo paisaje que el pedido.

   La procedencia indica que fue adquirida en Nueva York y está en el museo de Cleveland, sin indicación clara de que represente el mismo paisaje que la imagen subida. [2]
   Visualmente, la obra muestra un paisaje con rocas y bambú en tinta, pero no se puede confirmar que sea el mismo paisaje que el pedido.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “East Asian paintings from China, Korea, and Japan were frequently conceived as sets of multiple images. These sets might have been composed for specific palace or temple rooms, or to portray a specific theme, such as the four seasons. Over time, the original intent of such sets is often lost through damage, changes in ownership, or a variety of other reasons. 

The identity of the artist can also be lost, but then, sometimes, retrieved. This pair of ink paintings has traditionally been labeled as Japanese and attributed to the 16th-century painter Genga. Since there are no seals or signature of the artist on the painting, this attribution was based on comparisons of brush style with paintings known to be by Genga. More recent study indicates that while the 16th century is an appropriate time frame for the pair, the precise cultural identity of the artist is not certain after all. The dark, eccentric shapes of the rocks and bamboo clusters and the dramatic tonal contrasts evident throughout the composition point to either Korean authorship or influence upon a Japanese painter of the period.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1975.71.1 · CC0 1.0
   [2] “(Sotheby Parke Bernet, Inc., New York, NY)
The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, OH”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1975.71.1 · CC0 1.0

4. **Thatched Hut by Water's Edge**
   c. 1500–1573 · hanging scroll; ink on paper
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1997.125

   La obra es de un artista japonés del período Muromachi, que se interesó en la cultura coreana y china, copiando técnicas y efectos de pinturas continentales. [1]
   La pintura representa una imagen idealizada de un retiro de un erudito chino en el campo, con un fondo brumoso que aporta un elemento japonés a la composición. [1]
   Se observa un paisaje que combina elementos chinos idealizados con atmósferas propias del interés japonés por las estaciones y la sensación del lugar.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Muromachi period (1392–1573) artists in Japan were keenly interested in Korean and Chinese culture. Paintings from the continent were avidly collected, studied, and copied for specific techniques and effects. Most painters, however, never had the opportunity to actually travel abroad. This painting presents a typical, idealized image of a Chinese scholar's retreat in the countryside. The misty background, however, brings a decidedly Japanese element to the composition. Japanese painters had long been interested in portraying the seasons and in suggesting the special atmosphere of a place.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1997.125 · CC0 1.0

5. **Farming and Herding Buffalo in Summer**
   Kano Hideyori · mid- to late 1500s · hanging scroll; ink and light color on paper
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/2015.594

   El pintor Hideyori es conocido por escenas de género japonesas que representan actividades humanas en diferentes estaciones, con un enfoque en la prosperidad y el ciclo anual. [1]
   La obra muestra una escena de verano con personas trabajando en el campo y cuidando búfalos de agua, típica de la pintura japonesa de género. [1]
   No se menciona ni se observa que esta obra represente el mismo paisaje que la imagen subida ni que sea una versión japonesa de ese paisaje.
   La obra está claramente ambientada en Japón, pero no corresponde al mismo paisaje que el pedido.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Hideyori is most famous as the painter of a very early pair of genre screen paintings depicting people enjoying autumn foliage at a shrine-temple complex in Mount Takao near Kyoto. In this scene, people are hard at work farming their fields and herding water buffalo in summer. Such scenes were often associated with promoting the ideal of a prosperous realm, and also with the activities of the 12 months. Historical sources are divided on the biography of painter Kano Hideyori, but many scholars now believe he was the second son of Kano Motonobu, head of the Kyoto-based Kano family atelier.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/2015.594 · CC0 1.0
